t: #3877 Minimum Removals to Achieve Target XOR — Subset XOR DP
o: We must keep a subset whose XOR equals target while removing as few elements as possible, i.e., keep as many as possible. XOR values are bounded by 16383 (elements <= 1e4), so a knapsack-style DP over XOR values works: dp[x] = maximum subset size achieving XOR x. Answer is n - dp[target], or -1 if unreachable. Empty subset gives XOR 0, so target 0 is always achievable. Example: [1,2,3], target 2 -> keep {1,3} (size 2), remove 1 element.
k: Minimizing removals = maximizing the size of a subset with XOR equal to target.
XOR of values <= 1e4 stays below 2^14, so a 16384-entry DP table suffices.
dp starts as dp[0] = 0 (empty subset) and processes each element like 0/1 knapsack.

a.n: Approach 1: Knapsack DP over XOR values
a.i: For each number, every previously achievable XOR x can extend to x ^ num with one more kept element. Track the maximum kept-count per XOR value; read off dp[target] at the end.
s: Initialize dp[0] = 0 and dp[x] = -infinity for x > 0.
For each num, copy dp to nd; for each reachable x, update nd[x ^ num] = max(nd[x ^ num], dp[x] + 1).
After all elements, return n - dp[target] if dp[target] is reachable, else -1.
a.t: O(n * 16384) — about 6.5e5 state updates for n = 40.

w: With n <= 40, meet-in-the-middle over two halves (2^20 subsets each, hashing XOR to max kept size) also works and is worth mentioning. Pitfalls: forgetting the empty subset gives XOR 0 (target 0 answer can be 0 removals only if full-array XOR is 0, otherwise some removals), and iterating in-place without a snapshot, which would allow reusing the same element twice. Follow-up: count the number of minimum-removal subsets.
